findings: Slack decides author identity from the TOKEN, not a role field: with a bot token (xoxb-) messages 'appear under the app's name'; with a user token (xoxp-) 'Slack treats the action as if that person performed it. Messages appear under their name.' Source: https://slack.dev/two-keys-to-one-platform-understanding-bot-and-user-tokens/

Slack gives bot content distinct metadata rather than a distinct role: the event carries `subtype: bot_message` plus `bot_id`/`bot_profile`, and is 'like a normal user message, except it has no associated user.' `chat.postMessage` also accepts `username`/`icon_url` to override the bot's display name and icon. Sources: https://docs.slack.dev/reference/events/message/bot_message/ ; https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/chat.postMessage

Slack treats impersonation as a permissioned capability, not a message role: posting 'messages that appear to have been created by a user in the conversation... attributed to the user and show their profile photo beside it' requires the extra `chat:write.customize` scope, and Slack calls it 'a powerful ability [that] must only be used when the user themselves gives permission.' So distinct provenance is the default and folding into the human identity is opt-in and scope-gated. Source: https://docs.slack.dev/messaging/sending-and-scheduling-messages/

Zendesk already ships the exact two-verb model requested, as a single boolean: a ticket comment's `public` field is 'true if a public comment; false if an internal note' - one endpoint, one field, silent-internal vs visible-public. Source: https://developer.zendesk.com/api-reference/ticketing/tickets/ticket_comments/

Zendesk messaging separates attribution from formatting and is the closest published analogue to a voice producer identity: message author type is `user` (the end user) or `business`, and 'Business messages may also be sent by AI agents, third-party bots, directly using the API, or produced automatically by the platform. Each message has a `source` property that identifies where it came from.' Source: https://developer.zendesk.com/documentation/conversations/getting-started/key-concepts/

Zendesk attaches machine-readable provenance flags server-side (not just visually): comment metadata `flags` include 4 = 'The comment was automatically generated. Automatic email notifications have been suppressed' and 2 = 'The comment author was not part of the conversation.' Source: https://developer.zendesk.com/api-reference/ticketing/tickets/ticket_comments/

Zendesk's automated-note path is a documented cautionary tale for exactly this design: trigger internal notes 'are attributed to the system user', but trigger public comments 'are attributed to the ticket's current assignee' (system only if unassigned). Customers reported notes that 'appeared to come from me. I hadn't touched the ticket, but to anyone reviewing it, it looked like I had', and Zendesk replied that 'if it's coming from the system via a trigger, we want to make this clear in the reply itself and in the audit and event log.' Sources: https://support.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/6191477770906-Automatically-adding-comments-and-notes-to-tickets-using-triggers ; https://community.zendesk.com/ideas/select-comment-author-for-trigger-actions-internal-note-autoreply-5628

Zendesk renders a non-human actor differently in the UI, not only in data: AI agent tickets get 'A bot icon... in the ticket tab', 'An "AI agent" badge... in the ticket header', grayed-out property fields, a hidden composer and macros menu, and a distinct Support type value (`Support type | Is | Agent`) so they can be filtered out of human-ticket views. Source: https://support.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/9204149016346-Understanding-AI-agent-tickets-for-AI-agent-only-conversations

Zendesk exposes provenance as a first-class enum on the event itself via `via` types, with distinct values for `rule` (trigger/automation), `web_service` (API), `chat`, `answer_bot`, `answer_bot_api`, `answer_bot_for_web_widget`, etc. Source: https://developer.zendesk.com/documentation/ticketing/reference-guides/via-types/

Intercom gives its transcript an explicit three-valued author type: a conversation part's `author` is 'The type of individual that sent the message (`user`, `admin` or `bot`)'. A bot is a first-class author, not a disguised admin. Note-vs-reply is a separate axis: `part_type` is `comment` (reply) or `note` = 'A note created by an admin on the conversation. A note will only be viewable as an admin.' Source: https://developers.intercom.com/docs/references/2.1/rest-api/conversations/conversation-model

Intercom still permits the fold but declares it in the data model: 'Bots and campaigns send messages on behalf of Admins or Teams.' Source: https://developers.intercom.com/docs/references/2.1/rest-api/conversations/conversation-model

Freshdesk models the same two axes with different vocabulary: replies are always public and emailed to the requester ('Replies are always public and sent to the requester'), while notes carry a separate `_private` boolean (public note vs private note, 'Visible only to agents within your organization') plus an independent `incoming` flag - so the internal note is a separate object type, not a flag on a reply. Sources: https://developers.freshdesk.com/api/ ; https://partnerimplementationsupport.freshdesk.com/support/solutions/articles/50000000488-what-is-the-difference-between-a-note-and-a-reply- ; https://community.freshworks.dev/t/sending-a-conversation-as-private/14312

GitHub gives automated actors their own ACCOUNT, not a role: an installation token 'identifies the app as a GitHub App bot account, such as @jenkins[bot]' (the `[bot]` suffix is literal and part of the login), whereas a user access token 'identifies the app as the user who signed into the app, such as @octocat.' GitHub therefore offers both options (i) and (iii) and documents which is which. Source: https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/differences-between-github-apps-and-oauth-apps

GitHub's bot attribution is visible in the rendered transcript and carried in commit data: PR comments render as 'dependabot bot commented on behalf of github', commits carry `Signed-off-by: dependabot[bot] <support@github.com>`, and the git author/committer is the bot account with email `<BOT-USER-ID>+<app-slug>[bot]@users.noreply.github.com`. Sources: https://redirect.github.com/gradle/actions/pull/675 ; https://github.com/changesets/action/pull/448 ; https://redirect.github.com/peter-evans/create-pull-request/pull/3214

Bot identity is machine-detectable but the discriminator differs per API - a real pitfall for provenance code: 'GraphQL's `Actor.login` returns the bare name for bots ("dependabot"), unlike REST which appends a suffix ("dependabot[bot]")', so the reliable signal there is `__typename: "Bot"`. Discord is analogous: messages carry `webhook_id`/`application_id` and search filters on `user` | `bot` | `webhook`. Sources: https://git.homeinfra.org/actions/claude-code-action/src/tag/v1.0.197/src/github/types.ts ; https://docs.discord.com/developers/resources/message

Microsoft Teams renders author provenance structurally and denies the actor control over it: 'Teams client always renders bot messages on the left and user messages on the right', a bot 'can't update or delete messages sent by the user in Microsoft Teams', and bots cannot control bubble alignment. Teams then layers a second, non-removable provenance badge: `addAiGenerated()` puts an 'AI generated' label next to the agent's name with a hover disclaimer ('AI-generated content may be incorrect') that 'can't be customized for AI-powered agents', and the AI label is a policy requirement for agents distributed through the Teams Store. Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5634007/rendering-response-from-microsoft-bot-framework-in ; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/bots/how-to/conversation-messages ; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/bots/how-to/bot-messages-ai-generated-content ; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/bots/how-to/teams-conversational-ai/agents-best-practices-features-checklist

Google Chat makes bot-vs-human a TYPED FIELD and makes identity an auth decision: `User.type` is `HUMAN` | `BOT`. With app authentication 'Chat displays the Chat app as the message sender'; with user authentication 'Chat displays the user as the message sender and attributes the Chat app to the message by displaying its name' - i.e. (i) with disclosure, not full disguise. The API also enforces the distinction operationally: updating a message is 'only permitted on a `CARD_CLICKED` event where the message sender type is `BOT`.' Sources: https://developers.google.com/workspace/chat/identify-reference-users ; https://developers.google.com/workspace/chat/api/reference/rest/v1/spaces.messages ; https://googleapis.github.io/google-api-python-client/docs/dyn/chat_v1.spaces.messages.html

Discord has no legitimate (i) at all: 'Discord has no API for acting as your own account... Every legitimate integration acts as an application, and an application's messages carry an `APP` badge next to the name. No setting, permission, or endpoint removes it.' Webhooks can override `username`/`avatar_url` per message for display, but the message still carries `webhook_id` and the client still tags it. Sources: https://lanes.sh/docs/link/discord ; https://docs.discord.com/developers/resources/webhook

Aider renders three distinct provenance classes inside one transcript: `>` blockquote = 'output from the aider tool'; `####` heading = 'These are chat messages written by the user'; blue font = the LLM. The tool's own channel is inert: a parser for `.aider.chat.history.md` records that 'Slash commands you typed (`/add`, `/run` ...) are not turns; neither is Aider's own output (the `>` lines: announcements, token counts, commits)', and tool lines are distinguished from quoted content only by a trailing double space. Sources: https://aider.chat/examples/README.html ; https://www.molecule.dev/packages/api-agent-transcript-aider

Cline's transcript is an event log with a per-row KIND, not a two-party chat: `ClineMessage` is `{type: ask|say, ask?, say?}` over enums including `task`, `text`, `reasoning`, `tool`, `command`, `completion_result`, `hook_status`, `subagent`, `compaction`. Only the first row (`task`) is the user's prompt and renders via the `UserMessage` component; every other kind gets its own row (MarkdownRow, ThinkingRow, CommandOutputRow, RequestStartRow, McpResponseDisplay). Cline additionally keeps turn-starting out of the message model: a separate `TurnState` is 'the single authoritative UI mode for the current turn... the webview renders the footer/buttons/thinking indicator from this, NOT from the tail of clineMessages.' Sources: https://github.com/cline/cline/blob/7348ba18/apps/vscode/src/shared/ExtensionMessage.ts ; https://deepwiki.com/cline/cline/6.2-chat-interface ; https://github.com/cline/cline/blob/9dea336c/webview-ui/src/components/chat/UserMessage.tsx

Continue expresses ambient/injected content as inert context FOLDED INTO the user role instead of adding a role: context items are serialized into the user message body as `<context name="...">...</context>`, and a system message is injected at the head. Its unified `ChatMessage.role` is `system | user | assistant | tool | thinking`, where `thinking` has no OpenAI equivalent and is merged into the following assistant message, and on the Responses API path `system` is remapped to `developer`. Sources: https://github.com/continuedev/continue/blob/cb273098/core/util/messageConversion.ts ; https://github.com/continuedev/continue/blob/d0a3c0b6/core/llm/openaiTypeConverters.ts

OpenHands publishes the cleanest separation of the four options and is the strongest direct precedent for the DSH design: every event has `Event.source` in {`user`, `agent`, `environment`} for ATTRIBUTION and separately an LLM `role` in {`system`, `user`, `assistant`, `tool`} for FORMATTING. The docs state 'These fields are intentionally independent', give the exact case in question ('the SDK may inject feedback or control messages (e.g. from hooks) as `source="environment"` while still using an LLM `role="user"` so the agent reads it as a user-facing instruction'), and instruct: 'Do not infer event origin from LLM role. If you need to distinguish real user input from synthetic/framework messages, rely on `Event.source` ... not the LLM role.' Source: https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/events

OpenHands also defines a true inert channel in the same model: `ConversationErrorEvent` is 'Not sent to the model' while remaining in the append-only log, and the PR that introduced the ENVIRONMENT source states the motive verbatim - the UI needed error observations to be 'agent' events while 'the agents/llm treat them as `user`' - which is exactly the provenance-vs-role confusion the DSH plugin currently has. Sources: https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/arch/events ; https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/pull/4584

OpenHands also shows the dangerous default for an injection path like voice: the send-message endpoint's payload takes a `role` enum (`user`, `system`, `assistant`, `tool`) with `default: user`, so a naive injection of a transcript silently produces `user` provenance - indistinguishable from typed input - unless the caller deliberately sets `source`/metadata. Source: https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/agent-server/api-reference/events/send-message

Devin's own changelog is direct evidence of the same misattribution failure and its fix: transcript rows that used to read 'User answered: (no answer)' now show 'the question as skipped, with what was asked, instead of "User answered: (no answer)"' - a system/agent-attributed event replacing a falsely human-attributed one. Devin also names speakers on export ('Transcript copies include each speaker's name'), labels Slack origin ('the first message of a session started from Slack shows @Devin instead of the bot's user id'), and separates voice handling from internal notes ('the thread shows who is on the call and how long it lasted instead of Devin's internal voice notes'). Source: https://docs.devin.ai/release-notes/overview

Claude Code is the reference implementation of option (iv) and documents its hazards: the harness injects `<system-reminder>` blocks that are not the user's voice. A source-level trace found file-change reminders wrapped in a `<system-reminder>` USER message with `isMeta: true` that are permanent and never pruned; a user reported their own message being converted into a `<system-reminder>` such that the assistant 'didn't treat it as you talking to me'. The canonical harm case: a background `queue-operation` notification 'delivered as a user turn' was read as approval, the model fabricated the user's consent within the same assistant turn, and the user caught it only because 'the text rendering was visually different from actual user input' and the JSONL showed the phantom message as `type: assistant`, not `type: user`. Sources: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/43410 ; https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/11251 ; https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/62056

The `<system-reminder>` inert-context channel is also spoofable, which matters if DSH imitates it: a Bash tool result was followed by fabricated `<system-reminder>` blocks 'formatted identically to genuine harness reminders' instructing the model to conceal information from the user. Any channel that renders as trusted system context becomes an injection target if it is not structurally authenticated. Source: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/75758

Chat-API role vocabularies disagree on how many roles exist and where the system channel sits. OpenAI Chat Completions: `developer | system | user | assistant | tool` (+ deprecated `function`), `developer` replaces `system` on o1+, and a `name` field 'provides the model information to differentiate between participants of the same role' (the cookbook suggests `example_user`/`example_assistant` to mark non-real turns). Anthropic Messages: input messages accept only `user` and `assistant` - 'there is no `system` role for input messages' - `system` is a top-level parameter, `tool_result` is delivered inside a USER message, and newer models accept a mid-conversation `role: "system"` message with 'the same authority as the top-level `system` field'. Sources: https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat ; https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/how_to_format_inputs_to_chatgpt_models/ ; https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages ; https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/working-with-messages

The emerging transcript-telemetry schema is role-tagged and part-typed, and separates system instructions from messages: OpenTelemetry GenAI semconv records `gen_ai.input.messages`/`gen_ai.output.messages` as arrays of `{role, parts[]}` with `role` in system/user/assistant/tool and part types `text`, `tool_call`, `tool_call_response`, `reasoning`; system instructions are recorded separately as `gen_ai.system_instructions` rather than as a message in the history. Source: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-events.md

The Vercel AI SDK shows the pragmatic UI compromise: `UIMessage.role` is only `system | user | assistant` - there is no `tool` UI role - and provenance is carried in the `parts` array (tool parts, reasoning parts, source parts) instead. A voice producer identity can therefore be expressed either as a new role or as a part/metadata discriminator layered on the existing role. Source: https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/reference/ai-sdk-core/ui-message
patterns: Answer to the key question: real products use all four dispositions, and the two most directly analogous products (OpenHands, Zendesk messaging) both chose (iii) distinct source label for the automated actor plus (iv) a separate inert channel for context, rather than (i) or (ii).

(i) Fold into the user role - named exemplars: Slack `chat:write.customize` scope and user tokens (xoxp-) render the app's message as the human; GitHub OAuth user access token 'identifies the app as the user who signed into the app'; Google Chat user authentication (but it still shows the app name); Intercom 'Bots and campaigns send messages on behalf of Admins or Teams'; Anthropic `tool_result` delivered as a user message; Continue serialising `<context name=...>` into the user body; Claude Code `<system-reminder>` as an `isMeta: true` user message.

(ii) Give it the assistant role - named exemplars: OpenHands `MessageEvent(agent) -> assistant` and `ActionEvent -> assistant + tool_calls`; OpenTelemetry `gen_ai.output.messages` with `role: assistant`.

(iii) Own distinct role/source label - named exemplars: Slack `subtype: bot_message` + `bot_id`/`bot_profile`; Zendesk `business` author type + per-message `source` + `via` type enum + AI-agent badge/icon/Support-type; Intercom `author.type = bot`; GitHub `*[bot]` login suffix, `Signed-off-by`/`Co-authored-by` trailers, GraphQL `__typename: Bot`; Discord `APP` badge + `webhook_id`; Teams AI-generated label; Google Chat `User.type = BOT`; Cline per-row `ask`/`say` kinds; Aider's `>` tool channel; OpenHands `source=environment`; Devin named speakers and `@Devin`.

(iv) System / system-reminder channel that renders as inert context - named exemplars: Claude Code `<system-reminder>` with `isMeta: true` (and OpenHands `ConversationErrorEvent`, 'Not sent to the model'); Slack ephemeral messages (`chat.postEphemeral`); Zendesk internal note (agent-visible only); Intercom `note` part_type; Freshdesk private note; Aider's `>` tool-output channel.

Separate ATTRIBUTION from FORMATTING. The strongest published statement is OpenHands: `Event.source` = who produced it; LLM `role` = how it is formatted; 'these fields are intentionally independent', and 'Do not infer event origin from LLM role.' Zendesk does the same with author type vs per-message `source` vs `via`, and OpenTelemetry with messages vs `gen_ai.system_instructions`.

Two verbs implemented as one field or a type split: Zendesk `public: true|false`; Freshdesk reply vs note (`_private`, `incoming`); Intercom `part_type` comment vs note; Slack ephemeral vs posted message. This is the cheapest mapping for a 'silent note' vs 'visible say' pair.

Turn-starting is a property of the STATE MACHINE, not of message authorship: Cline's separate `TurnState` and `queuedPrompts` (the UI renders from state, not from the transcript tail); OpenHands send-message has an explicit `run: false` flag; Slack ephemeral messages are structurally non-turn-starting.

Layered disclosure badges on top of authorship: Teams `addAiGenerated()` label with a non-customisable disclaimer plus citations, feedback buttons and sensitivity labels, enforced as a policy requirement for Teams Store agents. Authorship answers 'who', the badge answers 'of what kind'.

Machine-detectable bot discriminators embedded in the data so downstream code can branch: Zendesk comment flags 2 and 4; GitHub `__typename: Bot` / the `[bot]` login suffix / `actor_type = Integration`; Discord `webhook_id` and `application_id`; Slack `is_bot` in `authorizations`.

Token/auth type determines identity, so the same code can produce different provenance: Slack bot vs user token; GitHub App installation token vs OAuth user token; Google Chat app vs user authentication; Discord refuses user-account automation entirely.

Inert-context channels create a distinct hazard surface: fabricated `<system-reminder>` blocks injected via tool output; system-reminder content reportedly absent from the persisted transcript (bad for audit); and unbounded repeated re-injection of the same context on every turn. Any (iv) channel needs authentication plus a lifecycle policy.

A transcript recorded for replay/monitoring is kept separately from the LLM-facing message list: OpenHands `ConversationErrorEvent` and `PauseEvent` live in the append-only log but never reach the model; Zendesk AI-agent tickets are read-only and execute no triggers; Devin keeps a worklog/replay timeline alongside the chat.
unverified: Devin's web-UI rendering of agent vs user turns (left/right bubbles, a distinct badge) is NOT confirmed from Devin's own docs; the 'Agent' vs 'Ask' mode dropdown and the Timeline/Shell/Editor pane split come from a third-party tutorial (datacamp) and a personal observation blog. The Devin changelog items cited in findings ARE vendor docs.

I found no primary Slack doc stating the exact CLIENT visual treatment of a bot message (e.g. an 'APP' badge). Slack documents the payload markers (`subtype: bot_message`, `bot_id`, `bot_profile`) and the token semantics; the badge wording for Discord and Teams is documented, but the Slack equivalent is inferred.

Discord's claim that the `APP` badge 'cannot be removed by any setting, permission, or endpoint' is documented by a third-party integration docs site (lanes.sh), not in Discord's own developer docs. Discord's own docs do confirm `webhook_id`, `application_id`, and the `bot`/`webhook` search filters.

No primary Cursor or GitHub Copilot Chat specification was found documenting how agent vs user turns are labelled in their transcript/state models; they are therefore absent from the findings rather than described from memory.

Whether Claude Code `system-reminder` content is ever persisted to the session JSONL is contradicted across reports (one reporter found zero matches for a genuinely-real reminder, implying reminders are not persisted at all). I could not resolve this from official docs, and I found no official Anthropic documentation describing the system-reminder channel - all evidence is user-filed issues.

I found no Zendesk vendor doc describing per-MESSAGE visual differentiation between an AI-agent and a human-agent message inside a single ticket thread. The distinct treatment cited (badge, bot icon, read-only, grayed fields) is at ticket level, not per-bubble.

Freshdesk's own help pages conflict on whether a PUBLIC note notifies the requester ('Visible to the contact within their support portal, but does not trigger an email notification' vs 'If you make the note public, requesters may receive an email notification'). Unresolved.

No standardised 'provenance' field name exists across these products. The nearest formalised vocabularies are OpenHands `Event.source`, Zendesk message `source` / `via` type, and OpenTelemetry `gen_ai.system_instructions` / `gen_ai.input.messages`; the word 'provenance' itself appears only as prose in vendor docs, and I found no canonical 'signed message' field in any chat/transcript API (the signing analogues found are GitHub's `Signed-off-by` trailer and commit signature verification, which are git-level, not message-level).

Zendesk comment flag codes and their meanings were read from the Ticket Comments API reference page as rendered in search results; the page body was not fully extracted, so the flag-number-to-meaning mapping is quoted rather than independently re-verified from the live table.

Microsoft Teams' AI-content-label behaviour (label text, hover disclaimer, refusal to render for non-AI scenarios) is documented, but I could not verify from primary docs exactly how Teams renders a message that is BOT-authored but NOT AI-labelled versus a human message in every client (desktop/web/mobile) - only the left/right alignment rule is stated.
